lesson.body:
Most smells in a glass fall into three groups, and sorting them helps you read a wine's style and age. Primary aromas come from the grape itself and where it grew. These are the fresh, obvious ones: fruit like cherry or lemon, flowers like rose or violet, and green notes like grass or bell pepper.

Secondary aromas are made during winemaking. Resting on spent yeast can give bread or biscuit smells; a softening step called malolactic fermentation adds the buttery note in some Chardonnays; and oak barrels lend vanilla, toast, or spice. (A few experts file oak under aging instead — either way, it's a winemaking choice, not the grape.)

Tertiary aromas build slowly as a wine ages in the bottle: dried fruit, nuts, leather, mushroom, or damp "forest floor." Older Riesling can smell of petrol, though that also depends on sun and ripeness, so young wines sometimes show it too. As a rule of thumb, dried and earthy usually means older — but some styles, like Amarone or tawny Port, taste that way when young by design. And faults (cork taint, for example) sit outside all three.

Explain where each group of aromas comes from
Use aromas as careful clues to a wine's age

deep_notes: Many primary aromas are hidden in the grape at first. They sit locked to sugar molecules with no smell of their own, and fermentation and ageing slowly set many of them free, which is partly why a wine can smell more expressive than the grapes it came from. Place matters too. The bell pepper note in Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc comes from compounds called pyrazines, which stay stronger when grapes grow in cool conditions or are picked less ripe.

In malolactic fermentation, bacteria turn sharp malic acid, the tart acid of green apples, into softer lactic acid, the acid found in milk. A by-product called diacetyl gives the buttery smell. Almost all reds go through this step, while many crisp whites skip it to keep their zing. Bread and biscuit notes come from autolysis: dead yeast cells slowly break down and release flavour, most famously in Champagne.

The traditional word for these age-driven smells is 'bouquet'. They form as acids, alcohol and fruit compounds slowly react with one another over the years. Fresh fruit fades and turns towards dried fruit, jam or fig. Whites can pick up honey and nutty notes, reds leather, earth and mushroom. Only a small share of wines gain from long ageing. Most bottles are made to be enjoyed young.

Riesling's petrol note comes from a compound called TDN. It forms from pigments in the grapes, and more sun on the grapes means more of it, which is why young Rieslings from sunny places such as Australia's Clare Valley can already show it. Amarone tastes of dried fruit from the start because its grapes are dried for months before fermentation. Tawny Port picks up its nutty notes from ageing in wooden casks before it is ever bottled.

deeper.body: Tertiary aromas come in two broad kinds. Oxidative ageing, where a little air slowly reaches the wine in wooden casks, gives nuts, caramel and toffee, as in tawny Port. Bottle ageing, with almost no air, gives different notes: leather, mushroom and forest floor in reds, and honey in whites. Knowing the route helps you guess how a wine was aged.
deeper.title: Two routes to age

opts: Bottle ageing with almost no air
deeper.q: Tawny Port smells of nuts and caramel. Which kind of ageing gave it those notes?
deeper.why: Tawny Port ages in wooden casks where a little air reaches it. That slow oxidation gives nuts, caramel and toffee.

deeper.body: The lees are the spent yeast that settles at the bottom of a tank or barrel. Some winemakers stir them back through the wine, a step the French call bâtonnage. It gives a rounder, creamier texture as well as bread and biscuit notes. Muscadet labelled 'sur lie' has rested on its lees through the winter before bottling, which gives it extra texture and flavour.
deeper.title: Stirring the lees

deeper.q: Which of these can time on the lees give a wine?
deeper.why: Lees contact adds creaminess and bread or biscuit notes. Leather and mushroom come from age, violet from the grape.

deeper.body: Some grapes wear their primary aromas loudly. Gewürztraminer smells of lychee and rose, Muscat of fresh grapes, and Sauvignon Blanc of gooseberry and cut grass. Others, such as Chardonnay, are fairly neutral, so the winemaking shows through more clearly. That is one reason Chardonnay so often carries secondary notes like butter, vanilla and toast.
deeper.title: Loud grapes and quiet grapes

deeper.why: Chardonnay is fairly neutral, so winemaking notes like butter and oak show through clearly. Gewürztraminer and Muscat are the loud ones.

v2.body:
**Émile Peynaud**, a scientist in Bordeaux, France, is often called the father of modern wine science. He got growers to pick riper grapes, sometimes two weeks later than usual. He showed wineries how to control a softening step many treated as a disease. He kept the word bouquet for smells only time can bring. Grape, winery, time: the three layers of this lesson.

Most smells in a glass fall into three groups, and each comes from a different stage of a wine's life. Sorting them helps you read a wine's style and its age. **Primary aromas** come from the grape itself and where it grew. These are the fresh, obvious ones:
• fruit, like cherry or lemon
• flowers, like rose or violet
• green notes, like grass or bell pepper

The place changes the primary smells. Chardonnay from a cool place tends to smell of apple and pear; from a warmer one, of peach and melon; from a very warm one, of banana and mango. Green notes like bell pepper stay stronger when grapes grow in cool conditions or are picked less ripe.

**Secondary aromas** are made during winemaking. Yeast, the tiny living things that turn sugar into alcohol, dies when done. Resting on this dead yeast, the **lees**, can give bread or biscuit smells. A softening step called **malolactic fermentation**, the one Peynaud tamed, turns the tart acid of green apples into the softer acid of milk, and adds the buttery note in some Chardonnays. Oak barrels lend vanilla, toast or spice, and new barrels give more than old ones. (Some systems file oak under ageing instead.) Chardonnay has a fairly neutral, quiet smell, so this shows clearly: without oak, it smells mostly of fresh fruit; with malolactic fermentation and oak, it adds butter, vanilla and toast.

**Tertiary aromas** build slowly as a wine ages in the bottle, as its acids, alcohol and fruit compounds react. Fresh fruit fades towards dried fruit, jam or fig. Reds pick up leather, mushroom or damp forest floor; whites, honey and nuts. The traditional word for these smells is **bouquet**. Only a small share of wines gain from long ageing; most are made to be enjoyed young.

Dried and earthy usually means older. But smells are clues, not proof. Amarone, an Italian red, tastes of dried fruit when young, because its grapes are dried for months before fermentation. Tawny Port, a sweet wine from Portugal, gets nutty notes from ageing in wooden casks. Older Riesling can smell of petrol, but sun and ripeness matter too, so young ones sometimes do. And faults, such as **cork taint**, which makes a wine smell musty, like wet cardboard, sit outside all three groups.
deep_notes: The scientist was Émile Peynaud. He taught at the University of Bordeaux and advised many of the region's wineries. In his day, many cellars treated malolactic fermentation as a disease of wine; he showed them how to encourage and control it instead. He pushed growers to pick later, sometimes by up to two weeks, and to sort out rotten or underripe grapes. He described an old wine's bouquet as a harmony of many small notes, in which no single smell is easy to pick out.

The three groups follow the order in which smells arrive in a wine's life, which is why tasting notes often run fruit first, then cellar, then age. The borders are not always neat. Oak is the classic case: some tasting systems count its vanilla and toast as secondary, because the winemaker chose the barrel, while others count them as tertiary, because they come with time in wood. Either way, they do not come from the grape.

Many primary aromas are hidden in the grape at first. They sit locked to sugar molecules with no smell of their own, and fermentation and ageing slowly set many of them free, which is partly why a wine can smell more expressive than the grapes it came from. That is also why tasting a grape straight off the vine tells you only part of what its wine will smell like.

Bell pepper is the clearest case of place shaping a primary smell. Its compounds, called methoxypyrazines, break down in sunlight as grapes ripen, so the note stays stronger in cool conditions or when grapes are picked less ripe. Chardonnay works the other way round: the grape itself is fairly neutral, so its smell follows the warmth of the place, from crisp apple and pear in cool vineyards to ripe tropical fruit in hot ones.

In malolactic fermentation, bacteria do the work rather than yeast. A by-product called diacetyl gives the buttery smell. Almost all reds go through this step, while many crisp whites skip it to keep their zing. Bread and biscuit notes come from autolysis: dead yeast cells slowly break down and release flavour. The longer a wine rests on its lees, the stronger these notes become, most famously in Champagne.

To check whether a note is secondary, ask whether the grape alone could have made it. Butter, bread, vanilla and toast could not: they point to choices made in the winery. Fruit, flowers and green notes could. Spice is the tricky one. Pepper can come from the grape itself, while clove-like notes more often come from toasted oak. So a spicy note alone rarely tells you which layer it belongs to.

These smells form as a wine's acids, alcohol and fruit substances slowly react with one another over the years, so they cannot be hurried. Only a small share of wines gain from long ageing, and most bottles are made to be enjoyed within a few years. A wine kept too long can lose its fruit altogether and taste dried out. So long ageing suits wines with plenty of fruit, acid or tannin (the drying feel of strong tea) to begin with.

Riesling's petrol note comes from a compound called TDN, which forms from pigments in the grapes; more sun means more of it, so young Rieslings from sunny places can show it. Amarone's grapes dry for months before fermentation. Tawny Port picks up nutty notes in wooden casks before bottling. Cork taint, caused by a compound called TCA, belongs to no layer at all: it is something that went wrong.

deeper.body: Tertiary aromas come in two broad kinds. Oxidative ageing, where a little air slowly reaches the wine in wooden casks, gives nuts, caramel and toffee, as in Tawny Port. Bottle ageing, with almost no air, gives different notes: leather, mushroom and forest floor in reds, and honey in whites. Knowing the route helps you guess how a wine was aged.

deeper.body: Some labels tell you about the lees. Muscadet, a white from the western end of France's Loire Valley, labelled 'sur lie' (French for 'on the lees') has rested on its lees through the winter and is bottled straight off them. That gives it a little extra texture and a subtle bready note, unusual in such a light, crisp white. Some winemakers stir the lees for a creamier feel; here they are simply left to rest.

Others, such as Chardonnay, are fairly neutral, meaning quiet, so the winemaking shows through more clearly. That is one reason Chardonnay so often carries secondary notes like butter, vanilla and toast.
